column1: # Curated word → emoji for the suggestion strip.
# These win over auto-generated names from Unicode/CLDR: "dog" is 🐶 rather
# than 🐕, "lol" is not a Unicode name at all, and a handful of short names
# people type (poop, thumbsup, smiley) are not in the spoken name.
# Chat slang and everyday associations live here. Distinctive names
# (flamingo, saxophone, abacus) are generated — do not duplicate them.
# Spoken forms, for SpokenEmoji ("crying emoji" → 😭). Keys here have their
# spaces removed, exactly like the generated ones, so "heart eyes emoji" looks
# up `hearteyes`. Most of these are unreachable by typing — nobody types
# "hearteyes" — so they cost the strip nothing and are the phrasings people
# actually say out loud. Measured against the shipped table, these were the
# common ones it answered with the words instead of the glyph.
# Phrases where the walk would otherwise resolve a shorter suffix and leave the
# rest of what was said stranded in front of the glyph — "face with tears of
# joy emoji" became "face with 😂", which is worse than not converting at all.
# Adding the whole phrase lets the longest-match rule do its job. The last few
# are the plain "<feeling> face" forms people say but Unicode does not name.
# Numbers. The only two digits in this file, and the reason the loader accepts
# them: a speech model writes someone saying "hundred" as "100" about as often
# as it writes the word, and "a hundred" strands its article on the walk the
